The US-Europe Income Growth Gap
Who Benefited?
Author: Pier Paolo Taddonio  |  Date: November 2026  |  Version: 2.08
Switch to landscape mode if you are reading this on a small screen

1. Introduction¶

1.1. Objective¶

The objective of this paper is to determine whether the income per capita outperformance of the United States relative to Europe was broadly shared across the income distribution or concentrated in a small part of the population.

1.2. Context¶

Real income per capita growth in the US has outpaced Europe's over the past decades. This gap is one of the main arguments to criticize Europe for doing too little to boost growth and to advocate adopting a more US-style economic model. This typically implies giving up some social advantages currently standard across Europe.

It is fair to assume that most Europeans would be willing to give up those if doing so were offset by higher income growth, if that deal was on the table. The US's recent experience offers the clearest evidence on whether that trade-off actually delivers for the majority of the population, or only part of it.

1.3. Scope¶

For the sake of this study, Europe is defined as the group of countries at the start of the Eurozone, not taking into account any addition after its creation (so Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain). This covers the biggest part of the European Union population (~70%) and GDP (~80%), offers standardised statistics and eliminates currency conversion issues. It is labelled EUZ here.

The time span considered starts in 2000 and ends in 2024, the most recent year for which comprehensive data are available.

This analysis uses pre-tax income statistics as opposed to disposable income, which is measured after taxation and transfers.

The objective is to focus on the impact of market forces rather than the effect of policy interventions.

1.4. Methodology¶

We compare income growth per capita between the USA and the Eurozone across the full income distribution. The population is divided into ten equal deciles based on income per capita, ranked in ascending order. Each decile represents 10% of the population: the first decile [0–10%] comprises those with the lowest incomes, progressing to the tenth decile [90–100%] representing the highest earners. We will label the first decile [0–10%] D01, the second D12 and so on up to the last decile [90–100%] labeled as D90.

To compare growth patterns, income changes are first expressed as indices anchored at 100 for the start of the period. This approach strips out baseline income differences so we're comparing percentage changes, not dollar (or euro) amounts.

In the following chart for example, the income data used is in USD for the USA and EUR for the Eurozone and income growth is computed in each region relative to its own currency value at the beginning of the period. There are no exchange rates involved in any way.

The chart displays real gross national income per capita growth for the USA (in blue) and the Eurozone (in orange) from 2000 to 2024.

By the end of the period, the USA index reached 137, a cumulative gain of 37%, while the Eurozone index ended at 122, reflecting 22% growth.

Annual bars (in light blue in the background) track the growth differential between the two regions year by year. Each bar represents the difference between the growth in the USA and the growth in the Eurozone in a particular year. For example the first bar represents the growth difference in 2001 which is approximately -1%, which means that in 2001 per capita income growth in the Eurozone was approximately 1% higher than in the USA.

These bars reveal that the gap did not evolve steadily but fluctuated considerably. For instance, two pronounced spikes stand out, one in 2012 and another in 2020, which means that in those years per capita income growth in the USA significantly outperformed.

Overall, the compounded annual growth rates (CAGR) are 1.3% for the USA and 0.8% for the Eurozone, a gap of 0.5% percentage points per year, which is displayed in the chart as the horizontal dashed light gray line.

A difference of half a percent per year in compounded annual growth is economically meaningful and a regular source of admiration for the performance of the USA economy.

2. Background¶

2.1. Population¶

Population growth since 2000 in the USA has consistently outpaced population growth in the Eurozone, year after year. While the Eurozone population has grown from 294m to 321m (+9% over 24 years), the USA population has gone from 282m to 340m, a growth of more than 20% and surpassing the size of the Eurozone.

2.2. Gross National Income¶

To study income distribution, Gross National Income is preferred to Gross Domestic Product. GNI is considered a people view of the economy while GDP is more about territory.
For instance GNI include income that residents earn abroad and exclude income that foreigners earn domestically.

Measured in "Local Constant Units" (meaning in local currency stripped of inflation), USA GNI reached 24.5 trillion $ in 2024, a growth of 65% since 2000, while Eurozone GNI growth was 12.3 trillion EUR in 2024, getting to +32% of growth.

2.3. Existing Data¶

For an overview of the available research and data, see the "Economic Inequality" report* published by Our World in Data, an initiative of the non-profit Global Change Data Lab. The report reviews various data sources and their methodological differences, and notably offers interactive visualizations for exploring the underlying datasets.
* Joe Hasell, Bertha Rohenkohl, Pablo Arriagada, Esteban Ortiz-Ospina, and Max Roser (2023)

The primary data sources are the World Bank, the Luxembourg Income Study and the World Inequality Database (WID).
Among these, the WID provides the most comprehensive database for this analysis and uniquely offers extensive pre-tax income data, even if its estimates rely on substantial modeling assumptions.

2.4. Existing Research¶

The 2020 research paper “Why is Europe More Equal than the United States?” partially addresses our question in page 23:

A more detailed picture of the distribution of growth in Europe and the US is displayed in Figure IIIb, which plots the average annual income growth rate by percentile in the two regions from 1980 to 2017, with a further decomposition of the top percentile. Average income growth has been slightly higher in the US (1.4% per year) than in Europe (1.1%) in the past four decades, yet this average gap hides substantial differences throughout the distribution. The average pretax income of the top 0.001% grew at a rate of 3.7% in Europe as a whole and as much as 5.4% per year in the US. Meanwhile, low-income groups have benefited significantly more from macroeconomic growth in Europe than in the US: the average income of the bottom 50% grew positively in Europe, while it stagnated in the US and even declined for the bottom 30% of the population. The two growth incidence curves cross at the 67th percentile, that is, while average pretax income growth has been higher in the US than in Europe, it has been lower for the bottom 67% of the US population than for all corresponding European income groups. *

* Thomas Blanchet, Lucas Chancel, Amory Gethin (2020). “Why is Europe More Equal than the United States?”. In: World Inequality Lab Working Paper, page 23.

According to this paper, between 1980 and 2017:

  • the bottom two-thirds (in income terms) of Europe's population experienced faster pre-tax income per capita growth than the U.S. equivalent,
  • the top earners in the US did much better than their European counterpart (they didn't do too bad either),
  • as we know that, on aggregate, the US has outperfomed Europe on income per capita growth, it means that all the outperformance was concentrated among top US earners.

Even if the scope of this paper is different from ours (Eurozone vs Europe, 1980-2017 vs 2000-2024), it gives a baseline for our analysis.

3. Analysis¶

3.1. Comparing Growth Dynamics across Income Deciles¶

The following charts represent the breakdown into the various income deciles of the very first chart. We are still comparing income growth across the U.S. and the Eurozone from 2000 to 2024, but for each income decile separately instead of the economy as a whole.

The following table gives a summary of the CAGR difference per decile.

According to this data, the U.S. has outperformed for top earners, but also for low earners, while the middle deciles exhibit a similar performance between the U.S. and Europe (the CAGR difference is close to 0).

Sensitivity analysis¶

The charts show that yearly growth-rate differences between the two regions fluctuate erratically across all deciles, displaying sharp bidirectional spikes without any systematic trend.

This volatility warrants a sensitivity analysis to make sure that our conclusions do not depend on a specific period, but are consistent within different time frames.

This table shows that the 2 lowest decile are very sensitive to the period chosen, and while they can experience some positive periods, they also witness some that are decidedly much worse. We can't therefore draw a definitive conclusion on these deciles.

The rest of the deciles though are more stable.
The high earners consistently do better in the U.S. than Europe, roughly outperforming by 0.5% on average, same as the full period figure.
The middle deciles are however surprisingly slightly worse in the USA than the Eurozone (small negative CAGR differences) in many periods. We can at least conclude that, for this part of the population, income growth in the USA is similar at best to that of the Eurozone.

3.2. Addressing the Low Base Effect¶

The analysis above treats every decile in isolation, and examines its own growth, relative to its own starting point.

As the starting points of each deciles are very different, the previous view is tainted by the "low base effect", and hides the fact that a 1% growth for the lowest decile is much smaller than a 1% growth for the highest decile.

Another viewpoint looks at the additional income over the period in both regions and allocates it to the various deciles.

The additional income can be seen as the pie generated by each economy over the period (in their own currency and in real terms). The size of this pie is rebased to 100, and then split into the 10 deciles. The sum of these allocations is obviously 100% for each region. The result is shown in the top part of the chart below. It is the distribution of the growth in National Income across the income deciles of each region.

In the second step, we want to allocate the overall outperformance of the USA over the Eurozone to its own income deciles, with the following process, bearing in mind that, from 2000 to 2024, the USA National Income grew by 65% and the Eurozone one by 32% (see above):

  • the USA pie (representing the 65% growth) is divided in 2 parts, the first is the Eurozone equivalent part (made of 32% growth, so 32/65 ~ 49% of the total pie) and the second one is the rest and represents the USA outperformance part
  • the Eurozone equivalent part is distributed across the USA deciles with the Eurozone percentages, which could be seen as what would have happened to the USA if it had grown and distributed its income in the same way as the Eurozone
  • finally the outperformance pie is distributed across the deciles by computing the allocation needed on top of the previous one (the Eurozone equivalent) to reach the USA allocation.

The outperformance allocation is shown in the lowest part of the chart below.

The top part of the chart shows that the low base effect is significant in both regions. A totally egalitarian outcome would distribute 10% to each decile, and a more realistic but still fair outcome would see a gradual increase crossing the 10% threshold around the middle deciles. Here the top decile gets more than 40% of the incremental income in the Eurozone and more than 50% in the USA, and the 10% threshold is crossed as late as the (70%-80%) decile.

The bottom part shows that the distribution of the extra income in the USA is even more skewed towards the top earners that the distribution of the total income: the top earners get more than 60% of that extra income, and the bottom 6 deciles (a majority) get very little, meaning that their share of the pie is practically the same as in Europe.

3.3. Accounting for population growth¶

So far we have looked at each decile as a stand alone entity, as if we were dealing with 10 people and looking at how their salary were evolving and what share of the profit they earn.

In practice the deciles are buckets with a lot of people.

As a consequence, people can move between buckets, so that if they go up a bucket for example, they experience a much higher income growth than the figures computed above. If that dynamic is very different between the two regions, the extra income growth that the lowest earners in the USA experience could become higher (or lower).

Data on this movement between income deciles is hard to come by, so we have to come up with a model, and keep it simple.

We will disregard the movements between deciles of the starting population (for which we are measuring income growth, the 2000 population). They mostly even out anyway.

What can make a difference is population growth. If it's significant, depending of where it enters the income distribution, it will push around the existing population into other buckets.

The USA has had a much larger population growth than the Eurozone. The fact that it has managed to grow its income and at the same time increasing its population to such proportions is the outstanding performance. So, could this population growth in the USA change the conclusions reached above?

3.3.1 Modeling the decile distribution of population growth¶

As a reminder, the objective of this analysis is to compute the income growth of the people in the various buckets at the beginning of the period.

What we have done so far is equivalent to assuming that all the starting population stay in their respective bucket, and that the extra population enters in equal proportions in each bucket, so that there is no displacement of the existing population. That is unrealistic.

Population growth can be split into Natural (difference between births and deaths) and Migration (net between immigration and emigration). Data is readily available about that.

A basic model could assume that:

  • Natural population growth enters proportionally into each bucket, so that all descendants inherit the status of their parents
  • Migration enters only in the lowest decile, therefore assuming that all net migration is coming in at the lowest level of income

With such a model, the Migration part would push the original population upwards through the buckets, effectively giving them a higher income growth. The Natural part does not change the picture.

3.3.2. Application¶

The population growth split between 2000 and 2024 for the USA and for the Eurozone is approximately as follows:

Region Natural change (%) Net migration (%)
USA 45 55
Eurozone 0 100

We compute the effect of this population growth on the deciles distribution as follows:

  1. We start with the lowest decile and allocate there 1/10 of the Natural growth and all of the Migration; if there is no room left to reach the 2024 bucket population size, then it means that the whole original bucket population has moved upward; if there is room, it means that some original population has stayed in the same bucket.
  2. We continue with the next bucket, where we start to allocate 1/10 of the Natural growth and whatever is left of the Migration if it wasn't all allocated before. Again, whatever room is left determines the fate of the original population of that bucket - either they stay in that bucket or they move up.
  3. We propagate that process to all the buckets, and in doing so we track all the subsets of population that have gone up in buckets, so that we can compute their income growth.
  4. We compute the blended income growth for each original bucket, taking into account the share that has gone up and the share that has stayed. This gives us the average income growth of the 2000 population in each bucket.

The following barchart represent this diffusion process for the USA.

The distribution of the USA outperformance with this model is among the most extremes when compared to all the outcomes in the previous sensitivity analysis table. The conclusions do not change.

There are many models that could be used to simulate the allocation of the population growth into the various deciles, and for each the results would be different. Exploring different ones and performing a sensitivity analysis on them is beyond the scope of this paper.

4. Caveats and conclusions¶

There are many caveats to this analysis, to name a few:

  • the underlying data coming from the WID embeds quite a few assumtions that some would not agree to;
  • the analysis is based on income, not on wealth, and the effects of the latter are intuitively bigger in the U.S. than in Europe (via 401K portfolios for example);
  • different diffusion models could produce higher income increases where population growth is strongest (U.S.), pushing a bigger share of the population through higher deciles.

Even allowing for these caveats, the magnitude of the distribution differences between the income deciles is compelling and supports the conclusion:

From 2000 to 2024, US income growth outperformance over Europe has accrued largely to top earners; the rest of the distribution, the middle class included, got little and fared no better than in Europe. American outperformance distribution offers little ammunition for those arguing that Europe should emulate it.
